title: Marketing Science in Python
text:
Preface
Last month’s campaign drove a spike in sales, and the team is celebrating. But was it really the campaign? Temperatures rose that same week. A competitor ran out of stock. An influencer posted about the product. Even if sales increased, did the campaign actually bring in valuable new customers, or just shift purchases that would have happened anyway?
Even in 2026, these questions are still hard to answer. AI has sped up the creative side of marketing, like generating ad copy, producing banners, and building landing pages. Coding assistants have made it much faster to write code and run analyses. But the decision side has not kept up. Questions like “Did it work?” and “What should we do next?” remain just as challenging. In marketing, you can never measure or control every variable that matters. You have to make decisions under uncertainty, often on a tight timeline. This is where human judgment is most important.
This book is a practical guide to making marketing decisions more reliable, even when the data is messy. Three things set it apart:
This is the guide I wish I had when I started applying data science to marketing.

title: Marketing Science in Python
text:
Who This Book Is For
I wrote this book with three readers in mind:

Data scientists moving into marketing. You are comfortable with machine learning, but want to tackle marketing-specific questions like experiment design, uplift modeling, customer lifetime value (CLV), pricing, and marketing mix modeling (MMM), where generic ML playbooks fall short.
Marketing analysts who want to see the implementation. If you have read articles about MMM and causal inference, this book walks through the working code from start to finish.
Business professionals who use models without building them. You can skip the code and focus on the problem framing at the start of each chapter. You will see where each model applies and where it breaks, such as why a discount can boost revenue but erode margin, or why an MMM needs experimental calibration.

This is not an introduction to Python or machine learning. It is not a theory textbook, and it is not a book of digital marketing tactics. Instead, it sits at the intersection: data science applied to marketing decisions.

title: Marketing Science in Python
text:
How to Read This Book
Parts 1 and 2 set the foundation: what marketing science is, what marketing data looks like, and how to design analysis that leads to better decisions. Read them first. After that, you do not need to go in order. Pick the path that matches the question in front of you.

title: Part 1. Introduction
text:
Photo by Carlos Muza on Unsplash

Most marketing teams face a familiar set of questions: Who are our most valuable customers? Did that campaign actually drive results? Which products should we prioritize, and how should we price them? Where should we invest the next media dollar? The goal of every analysis in this book is to help answer these questions and support better decisions. In Part 1, I focus on the foundations: what makes Marketing Science distinct from general data science, and what marketing data really looks like before any modeling begins. These basics matter, because in marketing, the right approach depends as much on the business context and the quirks of the data as it does on the technical method.
After this part, you will be able to:

Define Marketing Science and explain how its success criterion differs from general data science
Recognize how data ownership, granularity, and testability vary across the five industry contexts in this book
Use the funnel as a measurability map, and place the main marketing KPIs and datasets along it
Anticipate the three characteristics of marketing data and factor them into your analytical approach

title: 1.1 What Is Marketing Science?
text:
A Definition
In marketing, the gap between data science work and real business value often shows up in patterns like these:
None of these are hypotheticals; each is a pattern I have watched from inside marketing organizations, more than once. The first one, in particular, keeps reappearing in new forms: the store-level version, where an in-store program gets piloted in the stores that were already winning, is at least as common as the coupon version.
All three are different versions of the same problem. In the first, the analysis gave a clear number but missed the real cause. In the second, the model never reached the people who could use it. In the third, the analysis was done at a different level of detail than the business decision it was meant to support.
There is no villain in these stories. The campaign owner wants their campaign to succeed: that is their job, and wanting it is a healthy instinct in every role except the one measuring it. Some know exactly what sending coupons to loyal customers does to the lift number; many have simply never had a reason to think about it. Blaming either group gets you nowhere. What it does mean is that the data will keep arriving shaped by someone’s incentives, and that caring about the counterfactual is nobody’s job but yours.
That gap is the starting point for the definition we use in this book:
Marketing Science is the applied discipline of using data, statistics, and machine learning to improve business decision-making in marketing.
Figure 1 is the central idea of this book in one picture. The work is not done when the model is built. It is done when the analysis changes a decision, leads to a new action, and moves a business result. Every method in this book gets judged against that pipeline.
I did not start out thinking this way. Fresh out of grad school, I worked bottom-up: pull the data, explore it, model it, see what turned up, partly because finding things in data is simply fun, and partly because there was always a new method I wanted an excuse to try. At some point I presented a deck of findings I was quietly proud of, and the VP of Analytics stopped me with a line I still use on myself: don’t do analysis for the sake of analysis. It took a while to sink in. Nothing in that deck changed what anyone in the room already believed, and the new parts pointed to no action anyone could take. The findings were interesting to exactly one person: me. Learning to ask, before the analysis starts, whose belief it should change and what they would do differently is a skill of its own, and Part 2 of this book is largely about it. What eventually made the work interesting again was realizing that the hard problem was never the model; it was the three boxes to the right of Analysis. Figure 1 is that lesson, drawn as a pipeline.
This is also where Marketing Science parts ways with general data science. In general data science, success is often measured by prediction accuracy. Marketing Science still cares about accuracy, but accuracy is a means to an end: the real measure of success is the business result the analysis enables. There are corners of marketing where the two disciplines still coincide: ad-serving engines and recommender systems are optimization problems, and moving the metric is the result. This book deliberately focuses on the other side, analyses whose entire value is a better human decision (which budget to shift, which price to set, which customers to target), because that is where, in my experience, marketing teams still struggle the most, LLMs or not.
It also changes what counts as a good method. In academic research, novelty is the contribution; in decision work, a simple model the room can follow and reproduce usually beats a cleverer one that stalls in review. Where this book does reach for heavy machinery (the Bayesian MMM in Part 6 is not simple), it is because the decision demands it, not because the method is fashionable.

The definition applies across industries, but how you do the work (what data you have, which methods you use, how easy it is to experiment) varies a lot.

You do not need to memorize the table. What matters is seeing that the same marketing question can call for very different methods, depending on who owns the data, how granular it is, and how easily the business can test ideas.
For example, MMM is a well-established method in CPG with decades of history, while a SaaS team facing the same question would more likely lean on multi-touch attribution. Meanwhile, A/B testing is an everyday decision-making tool in app and e-commerce businesses, but running a rigorous A/B test in CPG is difficult. The reasons are rarely statistical. Relationships with retail partners and the operational preference for simple, uniform execution often rule out clean experiments, and the larger the organization, the more this holds. Part of the job, then, is getting the best measurement the constraints allow; Parts 3 and 6 show how.
In the U.S. market, the rapid growth of retail media networks such as Amazon Ads, Walmart Connect, and Instacart Ads is blurring these boundaries: CPG brands can now access near-user-level data through retail media. The table above is a snapshot, not a fixed map.
This book focuses on concepts that work across industries, while touching on industry-specific considerations where relevant.

title: 1.2 Understanding Marketing Data
text:
The Marketing Funnel
The rest of this book focuses on the work itself: framing questions, running analyses, and making decisions. But before any of that, we need to look at the raw material behind it all. In practice, marketing data is never a single table. It is a collection of sources, each reflecting a different slice of the customer journey, each with its own level of detail, timing, and gaps. To make sense of this, I break the landscape into three parts: where each dataset fits along the funnel, which KPIs and data types show up at each stage, and why working with this data is more challenging than it first appears.
Customers rarely buy on first exposure. They move (sometimes over months, sometimes minutes) from “not knowing the brand exists” to “buying” to “buying again.” The most common model of this journey is the funnel:
Awareness → Consideration → Conversion → Retention
The funnel is not helpful because customers always move through it in order; they often do not. Its real value is as a measurability map. As you move down the funnel, the data becomes more granular, measurement is more direct, signals arrive faster, and it becomes easier to run experiments.
This gradient explains why the Testability column appears in the industry table in Section 1.1. E-commerce and SaaS companies operate near the bottom of the funnel, where you can test behavior directly. CPG and brand advertisers work higher up, where the signals are noisier, slower, and more aggregated.
Whenever a KPI, dataset, or method shows up, in this book or in a stakeholder’s dashboard, the first question to ask is which part of the funnel it actually covers.

title: 1.2 Understanding Marketing Data
text:
Why Marketing Data Is Hard
A list of data sources is only a starting point. At first glance, these datasets look like standard data science inputs: tables to join, clean, and model. In practice, the real challenge in Marketing Science is not the complexity of the methods, but the nature of the data itself. Three characteristics show up in nearly every project, and each one shapes how you can apply the methods in this book.






Figure 2: Three characteristics of marketing data.




Characteristic 1: What’s measurable isn’t all that’s causal
Before a customer makes a purchase, they are influenced by many touchpoints: your ads and website, but also friends, competitors, the economy, the weather, and even their mood. Most of these influences never show up in your data. What gets recorded is usually the easy-to-measure activity: clicks, impressions, and page views. The real drivers behind a purchase often are not captured as data at all.
This asymmetry leads to the streetlight effect: teams focus on what is easy to measure, not necessarily what matters most.
Real business data is always messier than any dataset suggests. You need domain knowledge to fill in the gaps, and a clear causal framework to untangle what actually drove the results.


Characteristic 2: Analysis runs on business time
Marketing data is not built for research. It is a byproduct of daily business operations that have to keep moving. Campaigns launch, budgets shift, tags break, attribution windows change, and platform definitions get updated while the business keeps running.
In academic research, you can wait until you have enough clean data. In business, decisions cannot wait. An answer that arrives after the budget meeting is not useful.


Characteristic 3: Drivers rarely move independently
In a controlled experiment, you vary one thing and random assignment balances everything else across the groups. In real-world marketing, that almost never happens. The variables that drive sales usually move together, because something else is moving them all.
Consider a new product launch. TV ads, paid social, retail media, shelf-space expansion, and a price cut on the old product all happen at once, because management planned them for the same launch window.
Statisticians call this multicollinearity: when predictors move together, their individual effects cannot be separated cleanly. It becomes a major challenge in Part 6, when MMM tries to separate the effects of channels that always move together. The first step toward honest analysis is to recognize this constraint and be clear about what you can and cannot say.

title: Part 2. Analysis for Better Decisions
text:
Photo by Headway on Unsplash

The common failure is not wrong numbers. It is answering a question nobody needed answered.
Imagine spending two weeks preparing a deck: fifty slides, every KPI covered, clean charts, fresh data. The CMO listens for twenty minutes and then asks, “So what? What should we do?”
The problem is not the data quality. It is that the deck explains what happened, but not what decision should change. The CMO does not need a recap. She needs to decide where to move next quarter’s budget.
That is what it means to design analysis for better decisions: start with the decision, then design the question, metrics, and story around it.
This part builds those three skills in the order you would use them on a real project.
After this part, you will be able to:

Start analysis from business decisions, not metrics
Translate vague requests into clear business questions and hypotheses
Design KPIs that diagnose business gaps and avoid vanity metrics
Use KPI trees to connect outcomes, drivers, and actions
Structure findings as a decision story using the SCR framework

title: 2.1 Framing the Right Question
text:
Defining the Key Business Question
Before you even look at the data, get clear on the question your analysis needs to answer.
A useful question is not just interesting. It is tied to a real decision: who will do what differently if the analysis changes their mind?
Before starting any analysis, ask yourself:
“As a result of this analysis, who in which department will take what action, and when? How much business impact can we expect from that action?”
If you can answer this concretely, the analysis is probably worth doing. If not, you are likely heading into a fishing expedition, wandering through data and hoping something useful turns up.
A useful business question passes three tests:

Answerable: Can we answer it with available data before the decision deadline?
Actionable: Can we name the owner and the decision it will affect?

section: From Raw Request to Business Question
text:
From Raw Request to Business Question
Most analysis requests do not arrive as clear business questions. They usually start out vague.
The analyst’s job is not to take the request at face value. The real job is to translate that request into a decision.



Raw request
Better business question
Possible decision




Can you pull sales by channel?
Which channel explains the revenue gap?
Change next quarter’s budget allocation


Why is revenue down?
Which customer group, product category, or channel is driving the decline?
Decide which owner should act this month


How did the campaign perform?
Should we increase, maintain, or reduce spend on this campaign?
Reallocate campaign budget


Can you check retention?
Which customer cohort is at risk?
Launch a reactivation campaign



The raw request tells you what data someone wants. The business question tells you what decision the analysis should change.
crumbs: 3  2.1 Framing the Right Question

title: 2.1 Framing the Right Question
text:
Hypothesis-Driven Design
Once you have a clear question, do not jump straight into the data. A question by itself is still too broad. Form specific hypotheses to narrow your search.
For example, instead of asking ‘Why is revenue declining?’, break it down: ‘Is new customer acquisition falling?’, ‘Are repeat rates dropping?’, or ‘Is average order value down?’.
Before I write any SQL, I write five lines and sketch the output slide by hand:

Business question: Why did Q4 revenue miss plan?
Hypothesis: Existing customers purchased less frequently.
Metric to test: Purchase frequency by customer cohort versus last year and versus plan.
Output needed: A cohort-level trend chart with the largest gap highlighted: the chart that would convince the decision-maker if the hypothesis is true.
Possible decision: Launch a reactivation campaign for the affected cohort, or confirm the cohort is fine and stay the course.

If I cannot write the fifth line, or cannot sketch the fourth, I stop. The question is not ready.
Once the data starts coming back, hold the hypothesis loosely. If the data contradicts it, change course immediately. The moment you start cherry-picking data to fit your idea, you have left analysis and entered confirmation bias.
The workflow is simple: Question → Hypothesis → Output design → Data → Analysis → Decision. The important point is the order: start with the question, not the data.

title: 2.2 Designing KPIs for Diagnosis
text:
What Makes a Useful KPI
Even with a clear question and hypothesis, you still need to decide what to measure. KPIs turn the business question into measurable drivers and into evidence the decision-maker can actually use.
A useful KPI has two requirements.
Diagnostic. It points to where the business problem is likely coming from. A KPI may not tell you the exact action immediately, but it tells you where to investigate next. If no team can respond to the metric, it is just an observation.
Aligned with business objectives. It has a credible link to the outcome the business cares about. Correlation isn’t enough; you need to know that improving the KPI actually moves the end goal.
A common failure mode looks like this: an e-commerce team sets page views as its KPI. SEO drives up page views, but most of the new traffic does not buy, and revenue barely moves. Organic sessions to product and category pages would have been more useful, since that points the team toward traffic that is actually close to purchase.
crumbs: 4  2.2 Designing KPIs for Diagnosis

title: 2.2 Designing KPIs for Diagnosis
section: KPI Tree: From Outcome to Drivers
text:
KPI Tree: From Outcome to Drivers
A useful KPI hierarchy connects strategy to daily operations:

Business outcome: the top-level result the business cares about (revenue, profit, market share).
KPI (Key Performance Indicator): the intermediate metrics that drive the outcome (new customer acquisition, repeat purchase rate, average order value).
Action metrics: the operational levers teams control day-to-day (email send volume, ad impressions, page load speed).

This hierarchy forms a KPI tree. It breaks down the top-level outcome into the drivers that explain it. When the outcome moves, the tree tells you where to look first.






Figure 1: A KPI tree, from outcome to operational levers.



A good tree includes both lagging indicators that confirm results and leading indicators that give teams time to act.
crumbs: 4  2.2 Designing KPIs for Diagnosis

title: 2.2 Designing KPIs for Diagnosis
section: Using the KPI Tree to Diagnose a Gap
text:
Using the KPI Tree to Diagnose a Gap
“Can you just pull the numbers for our quarterly business review?”
It is one of the most common requests data teams get. It sounds like a simple data pull, but it is actually a chance to add value. The difference between a report and a review is diagnosis. A report just lists numbers. A review explains why they moved and what to do next.
An effective business review follows four steps:

Start with the top outcome. Are we on track versus plan, forecast, and last year?
Decompose the gap. Which branch of the KPI tree explains the movement?
Diagnose the driver. Which hypothesis best explains the gap?
Recommend the next action. What should the owner do differently?

If you do not include diagnosis and a recommendation, a business review is just a report.






Figure 2: A diagnostic KPI tree for a Q4 business review.



Numbers only mean something when you compare them. Always use at least one benchmark:

Year-over-year (YoY): compares the same period a year earlier, so recurring seasonality is not read as a change. “Revenue is down 5%” in January might be fine if it is always down in Q1.
Versus plan/forecast: measures execution against expectations.
Versus market/competitors: separates company-specific issues from industry-wide trends.

Audience Analysis
At the end of any analysis, you can either present a list of findings or build a story that drives a decision. A decision story explains what changed, why it matters, and what to do next.
Before building the story, answer three questions:
The gap between #2 and #3 is what your data has to bridge.

title: 2.3 Turning Data into Story
text:
Who makes the decision? Even if ten people are in the room, usually only one or two can actually act. Build your story for them.
What do they already believe? This becomes your Situation: the shared starting point your story builds on.
What action do you want them to take? This becomes your Resolution: the recommendation the analysis should produce.
crumbs: 5  2.3 Turning Data into Story

title: 2.3 Turning Data into Story
text:
The SCR Framework
A practical story structure is Situation → Complication → Resolution (SCR).
Situation. What is the current state? What background does the audience already know? Start with facts they already accept.
Complication. What changed? What is the problem? What are the risks if nothing is done? This is where you show why action is needed.
Resolution. What does the data show, and what do you recommend? This is the ask.
Before you build your presentation, write down these three parts clearly. If you cannot, the analysis is not ready.
crumbs: 5  2.3 Turning Data into Story

title: 2.3 Turning Data into Story
section: Example: Explaining a Revenue Miss to the CMO
text:
Example: Explaining a Revenue Miss to the CMO
Recall the opening of this part: the CMO sat through fifty slides and asked, “So what? What should we do?” Here is what she actually needed.
The CMO has to decide where to shift next quarter’s budget. That’s the decision the analysis should change.
Situation. Revenue is growing, and new customer acquisition is on track.
Complication. Q4 finished below plan. The gap comes from existing customers: purchase frequency among the cohort acquired during Q2 promotions dropped sharply, pulling down existing-customer revenue.
Resolution. This is not a broad acquisition problem. Keep acquisition spend stable, but launch a reactivation campaign for the Q2 promotional cohort and tighten future promotion targeting.
The story is no longer just ‘here are the metrics.’ It is ‘the revenue gap is a retention problem, not an acquisition problem, and the next action is reactivation.’ That is the version the CMO can actually act on.

title: Part 3. Causal Inference for Marketing
text:
Photo by Artem Beliaikin on Unsplash

“Did this marketing activity actually increase sales?” This part is about practical tools for answering that question. We’ll cover A/B testing, quasi-experiments, causal impact analysis for the actions that already ran, meta-learners for understanding which customers respond differently, and uplift modeling to help you target the people who actually change their behavior.
After this part, you will be able to:

Distinguish correlation from causation in marketing data
Design, run, and analyze A/B tests correctly
Estimate causal effects when randomization isn’t possible
Measure a one-off intervention that ran without a holdout
Estimate how a treatment effect varies from customer to customer
Identify which customers benefit most from a treatment using uplift modeling

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
text:
Selection Bias
Let’s consider a typical situation that many data scientists face in business. Imagine you’re assisting a colleague from the marketing team, and they say:
“The marketing team sent coupons to some users, and their purchase rate was twice as high as those who didn’t receive them. So, the coupons must have doubled the purchase rate!”
Would you agree with this conclusion? At first glance, you might be inclined to agree. But wait, what if you knew this additional detail?
“We sent the coupons only to customers who had purchased within the last 12 months.”
Now this raises a red flag. So what’s the potential issue here?
The key question is: what is the true impact of the coupons? If we distribute coupons based on intentional criteria, we can’t make a fair comparison between purchase rates. The customers who received the coupons might have made a purchase regardless. They were already more engaged, and may have been influenced by other factors like newsletters or social media. These factors introduce what’s known as selection bias: the distortion that arises when the treated and untreated groups aren’t comparable to begin with.
The 10-point gap between groups looks impressive, but most of it was already there before the coupons went out. The real lift from the coupon (the part that wouldn’t have happened otherwise) might be just a few points. The rest is selection bias: the coupon went to people who were likely to buy anyway.
You see this pattern all the time in marketing. Retargeting campaigns show high conversion rates, but that’s because they reach people who already visited your site. Email campaigns look great on revenue per recipient, but those emails go to your most engaged subscribers. In both cases, the treatment and the outcome are linked because of customer intent, not because the treatment caused the outcome.

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
text:
What Is Causal Inference?
So how do we move past these traps? This is where causal inference comes in.
Causal inference is about figuring out whether there is a cause-and-effect relationship between a specific action (the “treatment”) and its result (the “outcome”). Traditionally, it has been a cornerstone in fields like healthcare. For example, one common use case is assessing whether a new medication effectively treats a disease. In that context, administering the medication is the “treatment,” and the patient’s recovery is the “outcome.”
But causal inference isn’t just for healthcare. In e-commerce and marketing, “treatments” include actions like sending coupons, running advertisements, or sending direct mail campaigns, and “outcomes” are things like purchases, sign-ups, or revenue.






Figure 3: Treatment and outcome across healthcare and marketing.

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
text:
The Counterfactual
The main challenge in causal inference is that we can only observe one outcome for each individual. If we had a time machine, we could give a customer a coupon, then rewind time and see what happens if we didn’t give them the coupon. In the real world we can’t: we only ever see one version of the story for each customer.
This is where causal inference steps in: it lets us estimate the outcome that didn’t happen, known as the counterfactual.






Figure 4: The fundamental problem of causal inference.



Formalizing this makes the problem precise. The treatment effect for a customer is:
\[\tau = Y(1) - Y(0)\]
Here, \(Y(1)\) is what happens if someone gets the treatment, and \(Y(0)\) is what happens if they don’t. The problem is, we only ever see one of these for each person. If we just compare treated and untreated groups without accounting for this, we mix up the true effect with differences that were already there. That’s selection bias.

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
section: Why Not Just Run an A/B Test?
text:
Why Not Just Run an A/B Test?
You might wonder, “Why not just run an A/B test?”
In marketing, this approach is called A/B testing, and in the broader causal inference literature it’s also known as a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). It is often considered the “gold standard” for answering causal questions. Here’s how it works.
You randomly divide your customers into two groups: the “treatment group” and the “control group.” The treatment group receives the coupon; the control group does not. Say the treatment group’s purchase rate ends up at 40% and the control group’s at 20%. The difference, 20 percentage points, is the effect of the coupon.






Figure 5: A randomized controlled trial.



The critical point is randomization. By randomly assigning customers, we ensure that other factors (customer preferences, past behavior, channel exposure) are balanced across both groups. That balance is what removes the selection bias that would otherwise distort the comparison.

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
text:
Limitations of A/B Testing
So if we understand A/B testing, does that mean it’s always the perfect solution? Unfortunately, no. While A/B testing provides the strongest evidence available, there are many situations where it just isn’t feasible:

Opportunity loss. If you run an A/B test, half your customers won’t receive the new product or offer. That could mean missing out on sales and growth, an “opportunity loss” the business can’t always afford.
Time constraints. A/B tests can be time-consuming. They often require weeks or even months to gather enough data to draw reliable conclusions. That delay can mean missing a market window or losing a competitive edge.
Stakeholder complexity. A/B tests become harder when multiple stakeholders are involved. Not every client or partner has the resources or ability to execute one effectively.

When A/B testing isn’t an option, we have to fall back on observational data: data collected without any deliberate experiment.

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
section: Simpson’s Paradox: Challenges of Observed Data
text:
Simpson’s Paradox: Challenges of Observed Data
Observational marketing data can be misleading even when the pattern looks obvious.
Suppose we want to understand the relationship between email frequency and unsubscribe risk. We plot each subscriber by how many marketing emails they receive and whether they are likely to unsubscribe. In the aggregate data, the pattern looks surprising: subscribers who receive more emails appear less likely to unsubscribe.
At first glance, this might suggest that sending more emails reduces unsubscribe risk. But that conclusion should make us uncomfortable. For the same type of subscriber, sending too many emails should usually increase the chance that they unsubscribe, not reduce it.
So what is missing? Prior email engagement.
Marketing teams rarely send emails at random. Subscribers who often open and click emails usually receive more campaigns, because they are active and responsive. Subscribers who rarely engage often receive fewer campaigns, or are suppressed from some sends. These groups have very different baseline unsubscribe risks.
Once we segment subscribers by prior email engagement, the pattern reverses: within every engagement group, higher email frequency is associated with higher unsubscribe risk. (Low-engagement subscribers are more likely to unsubscribe overall, but inside each group, sending more emails still raises that risk.)
This is Simpson’s Paradox: the aggregate trend says one thing, while the pattern within comparable groups says the opposite.






Figure 6: Simpson’s Paradox: email frequency vs. unsubscribe risk.

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
text:
Confounding Variables
In the email example, prior engagement is a confounding variable: a variable that influences both the treatment (email frequency) and the outcome (unsubscribe risk). Failing to account for confounders can lead to misleading conclusions, including, as we just saw, a completely reversed effect. That’s why identifying and controlling for these variables is central to causal inference with observational data.






Figure 7: A confounder behind email frequency and unsubscribes.



The lesson: with observational data, always ask whether there is a confounding variable hiding behind the numbers.

title: 3.1 Causal Thinking
text:
Road Map for Part 3
Here’s the plan. The first job is to get a comparison you can believe. If you can randomize, A/B testing gives the most reliable answer. When you cannot, quasi-experimental designs reconstruct the comparison from how the treatment was assigned, and that includes the action that reached everyone on a known date, where the missing no-treatment path is forecast from the series’ own history. The second job starts once you have an effect you trust, and asks how it varies from customer to customer, so you can stop spending on people who would have converted anyway. That is what meta-learners and uplift modeling do.

title: 3.2 A/B Test Design
text:
Statistical Power
Your team just finished a two-week A/B test on the new checkout page. Everyone is eager to see the results. Then the numbers come in:
Treatment looks a little better, a 0.24-point lift. But a two-proportion z-test puts the p-value at 0.43:
So the team says, “Not significant. The redesign doesn’t work. Let’s move on.” That conclusion isn’t backed up by the data. A p-value of 0.43 doesn’t mean there’s no effect. It means the test couldn’t separate a small effect from random noise. The treatment might really be better; the data just can’t say. The gap between “no effect” and “we can’t tell” comes down to whether the test had enough power.
Statistical power is the chance your test will detect an effect of a specific size if that effect truly exists. Most teams aim for 80% power, which still leaves a 20% chance of missing an effect that large.
Imagine repeating the same A/B test many times. If the redesign has no real effect, the estimated lift will bounce around zero. If the redesign truly improves conversion, the estimated lift will bounce around the real lift. Power is the chance that the test lands far enough from zero for us to detect that effect.
For a low-conversion event like a purchase (say a 2% conversion rate), detecting a 0.5-point lift takes many thousands of users per group, and most teams run with far fewer. This is the part most teams underestimate: detecting small lifts usually requires far more traffic than intuition suggests.

text: Figure 1: Statistical power: the H0 and H1 distributions.

title: 3.2 A/B Test Design
text:
Calculating Sample Size
So how many users do you actually need? Sizing a test takes four inputs: the baseline conversion rate, the minimum lift worth detecting (the MDE), the false-positive rate you’ll tolerate (\(\alpha\), usually 0.05), and the power you want (\(1 - \beta\), usually 0.80).
The key intuition is:
\[n \propto \frac{1}{\text{MDE}^2}\]
If you want to detect half the lift, you need roughly four times as many users. In Python:
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

baseline_cvr = 0.02
target_cvr = 0.025
effect_size = abs(proportion_effectsize(target_cvr, baseline_cvr))

analysis = NormalIndPower()
required_n = analysis.solve_power(
    effect_size=effect_size,
    alpha=0.05,
    power=0.80,
    ratio=1,
    alternative="two-sided",
)
print(f"Required sample size per group: {required_n:.0f}")  # ~13,800
Detecting a lift from a 2% baseline to 2.5% needs about 13,800 users per group. In practice teams round up and pad for tracking loss and excluded users, so they would plan for roughly 15,000.






Figure 2: Sample-size sensitivity to the MDE.



The curve makes the main lesson visible: sample size does not grow linearly but climbs steeply as the target lift shrinks. This is why small improvements on low-conversion metrics are expensive to measure.

title: 3.2 A/B Test Design
text:
Decide Before You Launch
Before launching the test, write down four decisions:

Primary metric: which metric decides the test?
MDE: what lift is large enough to matter?
Sample size and duration: how much data will you collect before judging the result?
Guardrail metrics: what should not get worse (revenue per user, page-load time, support tickets)?

Writing these down up front guards against two habits that quietly inflate false positives: peeking (stopping the test the moment it looks significant) and metric fishing (reporting whichever of many metrics happened to move).

title: 3.2 A/B Test Design
section: CUPED: Getting More Precision from the Same Sample
text:
CUPED: Getting More Precision from the Same Sample
When the required sample is out of reach, you can’t always add more users, stores, or markets. CUPED (short for Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) can sometimes give you more precision from the same data by using information from before the experiment. Microsoft’s experimentation team introduced it in 2013 to make online experiments more sensitive without collecting more data (Deng et al. 2013), and it has since become a standard variance-reduction tool in large-scale experimentation.
The idea is simple. If a customer was already a high spender before the experiment, they will probably keep spending during it too, treatment or not. CUPED subtracts that predictable part of the outcome, so the comparison focuses on what actually changed during the test.






Figure 3: How CUPED removes pre-experiment variance.



In the figure, Customer A spent $100 before the campaign and $110 during it. Given that history you’d expect about $102, so the lift above expectation is just $8, not the full $110. Stripping out each customer’s predictable spend tightens the spread of outcomes without changing the average treatment effect, so the effect becomes easier to detect.
The same idea helps in store-level or market-level experiments. Suppose a retailer wants to test an in-store promotion. Randomizing hundreds of stores into treatment and control may be operationally unrealistic, and every store is different: some are larger, some have different customer bases, some are hit by local events. CUPED can use each store’s pre-experiment sales to remove part of that predictable store-to-store variation. It doesn’t create more stores or fix a weak design, but when pre-period sales strongly predict sales during the test, it can make a smaller store test more precise.
Formally, let \(Y\) be the outcome and \(X\) a pre-experiment covariate (e.g., purchases in the prior 30 days). The adjusted outcome is:
\[Y_{\text{CUPED}} = Y - \theta \cdot (X - \bar{X})\]
where \(\theta = \text{Cov}(Y, X) / \text{Var}(X)\). The variance of the adjusted outcome reduces to \(\text{Var}(Y_{\text{CUPED}}) = \text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2)\), where \(\rho\) is the Pearson correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\). If \(\rho = 0.7\), CUPED removes about half the variance, as much precision as doubling the sample would buy. Netflix later published case studies reporting similar variance reductions across its large-scale online experiments (Xie and Aurisset 2016). The most common covariate is the same metric measured in the pre-experiment period, which usually gives the strongest correlation.
In code, the adjustment is only a few lines. On a simulated campaign where pre-period spend correlates with in-experiment spend at about 0.75, it cuts the standard error of the lift by about a third:
import numpy as np

# df: one row per customer — pre_spend (prior 30 days), campaign_spend, treatment (0/1)
theta = np.cov(df["campaign_spend"], df["pre_spend"])[0, 1] / df["pre_spend"].var()
df["cuped_spend"] = df["campaign_spend"] - theta * (
    df["pre_spend"] - df["pre_spend"].mean()
)

for metric in ["campaign_spend", "cuped_spend"]:
    t = df.loc[df["treatment"] == 1, metric]
    c = df.loc[df["treatment"] == 0, metric]
    se = np.sqrt(t.var() / len(t) + c.var() / len(c))
    print(f"{metric:15s} lift={t.mean() - c.mean():.2f}  SE={se:.3f}")
# campaign_spend  lift=0.97  SE=0.549
# cuped_spend     lift=1.07  SE=0.364   (33.7% smaller SE — like a much bigger sample)
The point estimate shifts slightly (0.97 → 1.07): CUPED removes the part of the raw gap caused by a chance pre-period imbalance between the groups, so it still targets the same true effect while the interval tightens. The companion notebook simulates df end to end (reporting p-values, which here drop from 0.08 to 0.003) so you can change the correlation and watch the precision gain shrink or grow.

title: 3.2 A/B Test Design
text:
When a Test Is Inconclusive
Return to the checkout test. The right question isn’t “was the p-value below 0.05?” It’s “was the test precise enough to rule out an effect we’d care about?”
Look at the confidence interval. The observed lift was +0.24 points, but the 95% interval runs from −0.36 to +0.84 points, wide enough to include both a small loss and a sizable win. That test is inconclusive: it hasn’t shown the redesign works, but it certainly hasn’t shown it doesn’t. Only when the interval is narrow and excludes any lift worth shipping can you reasonably set a treatment aside.
A non-significant result, in other words, is not automatically a failed treatment. It may simply mean the test was too small, too noisy, or run during an unusual period.

title: 3.2 A/B Test Design
text:
Key Takeaways

A non-significant result is not evidence of no effect. An underpowered test cannot separate a real lift from noise, so before declaring a treatment dead, ask whether the test could have detected an effect you care about.
Sample size scales with \(1/\text{MDE}^2\). Detecting half the lift takes roughly four times the users, which is why small improvements on low-conversion metrics are expensive to measure.
Decide four things before launch: the primary metric, the MDE, the sample size and duration, and the guardrail metrics. Writing them down protects you from peeking and metric fishing.
Judge inconclusive tests by the confidence interval, not the p-value. If the interval still includes lifts worth shipping, the test has not failed; it just has not answered yet.
When you cannot collect more data, CUPED can buy precision from pre-experiment data. At a correlation of 0.7 it removes about half the variance, as much as doubling the sample.

Xie, Huizhi, and Juliette Aurisset. 2016. “Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments: Case Studies at Netflix.” Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD ’16), 645–54. https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939733.

title: 3.3 Quasi Experiments
text:
Which Design Fits Your Situation?
A/B testing is the gold standard for measuring cause and effect. Randomize who gets the treatment, and the control group tells you what would have happened without it. But you can’t always run one. As Section 3.1 covered, there are plenty of reasons an A/B test isn’t an option.
When you can’t randomize, you use a quasi-experiment. A quasi-experiment estimates cause and effect without random assignment. It works with whatever comparison the business process left behind: a cutoff, a rollout that skipped some units, a launch date. That last part is the catch. A non-random rollout isn’t automatically a usable quasi-experiment. It has to leave a comparison whose assumptions you can defend, and each design in this chapter comes with the assumption you’ll have to defend.
This chapter covers three designs: Regression Discontinuity (RDD), Difference-in-Differences (DiD), and Synthetic Control. Each one needs untreated units to compare against: a control group of stores that didn’t get the display, or a pool of stores to blend into one. The fourth design, CausalImpact, is for when there are no untreated units at all. It gets the next chapter.
Four designs is a lot to choose from, and the names don’t tell you which one you need. So let’s put them all on one concrete problem. A retailer has 100 stores. It rolled out a new in-store display and wants to know what the display did to category sales.
The first question is always the same: was the display assigned at random? If it was, the untreated stores are your control group and you’re back in Section 3.2. If it wasn’t, the way it was assigned picks the design.
Every row has the same 100 stores. What changed is how the display was assigned, and that decides both the design and the data you need: the running variable for RDD, a before-and-after panel for DiD, a long pre-period and a pool of untreated stores for Synthetic Control. Fifty stores chosen at random and fifty chosen by the sales team can produce the same spreadsheet, and only the first is an experiment. That’s the rule for the whole chapter. The assignment picks the design. The data then decides whether the design is credible.
That table is one retailer’s five options. Figure 1 turns it into a router for any rollout: two yes-or-no questions, then a choice that depends on how much untreated data you have left.
The four designs aren’t four unrelated tricks, either. One of them, RDD, uses a cutoff and nothing else. The other three form a ladder. DiD borrows the trend of the control stores. Synthetic Control blends control stores into a better comparison when no single one will do. CausalImpact forecasts the comparison when there are no control stores at all. Each rung leans harder on a model. This chapter covers RDD and the first two rungs.

title: 3.3 Quasi Experiments
text:
Regression Discontinuity (RDD)
Core idea: right around the cutoff, the assignment is as good as random.
Start with the second row of Table 1. Instead of picking the stores, the sales team wrote a rule: every store above $1M in annual sales gets the new display. The pilot stores are now the biggest stores by construction. Comparing them to the rest would just measure what it’s like to be big.
But look at the stores near the line. A store doing $1.02M and a store doing $0.98M are about the same size, serve similar shoppers, and run similar promotions. Which side of $1M they landed on is close to a coin flip. RDD treats it as one. It compares outcomes just above the cutoff to outcomes just below it, and if category sales jump at $1M, the jump is the effect of the display. The same logic works for customers: if customers with at least $500 of past spend get a coupon, compare the $502 customers to the $498 ones.

When RDD doesn’t work
RDD needs a lot of units near the cutoff, because it uses only those. With 100 stores, maybe ten sit within a few percent of $1M, and that’s too thin to fit a line on each side and see a jump above the noise. With 20,000 customers near $500, it isn’t. That’s why RDD is mostly a customer-level tool in marketing: coupons or points based on past spend, lead-score cutoffs for sales outreach. Figure 2 shows that version.






Figure 2: Regression Discontinuity Design: a jump at the threshold.



Two more limits. The effect is local: the jump at $500 says what the coupon did for customers who spend about $500, not for customers who spend $5,000. And the units can’t be able to move themselves across the line. If a rewards program promotes customers to the next tier at $1,000 and customers know it, some will make one extra purchase in December to get over. If a store manager gets a bonus for hitting $1M, stores at $0.97M in November find a way to finish at $1.01M. Either way, the units just above the cutoff are the ones who tried harder, and RDD reads that as the effect of the treatment. A histogram of the running variable with a pile just above the cutoff is the tell. On a threshold like that, RDD can’t be used.

title: 3.3 Quasi Experiments
text:
Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
Core idea: compare changes, not levels. The control group’s change over time stands in for what the treated group would have done.
Now the third row of Table 1: the sales team picked 50 stores for the new display, and 50 comparable stores kept the standard shelf layout. You have category sales per store, before and after the rollout, for both groups.
The pilot stores went from $42k to $48k. So the display is worth $6k per store?
Probably not. The comparison stores went from $40k to $43k with no display at all. Something lifted the whole category by about $3k: seasonality, traffic, a competitor’s stockout. A before-and-after comparison on the pilot stores alone books that market growth as display effect.
So compare the two groups after the rollout instead. $48k against $43k is $5k. Is that the effect?
Also no. The pilot stores were already $2k ahead before anything happened, at $42k against $40k. The sales team didn’t pick at random, and a treated-versus-control comparison in the post period books that head start as display effect.
Each naive comparison fails on a different confound. Before-versus-after catches the shared time trend. Treated-versus-control catches the pre-existing gap between the groups. Take the difference of the two differences, and both cancel:

Pilot stores grew by $6k, comparison stores by $3k, and the difference is $3k. You get the same answer the other way around: a $5k gap after minus a $2k gap before. That’s Difference-in-Differences. The shared trend cancels out. So does any fixed difference between the groups. What’s left is the part of the pilot stores’ change that the comparison stores can’t explain.
In code, the estimate is just those two differences:
import pandas as pd

did = pd.DataFrame({
    "group":  ["Pilot stores", "Comparison stores"],
    "before": [42, 40],   # category sales per store, $k
    "after":  [48, 43],
})
did["change"] = did["after"] - did["before"]              # +6 and +3
did_estimate = did.loc[0, "change"] - did.loc[1, "change"]
print(f"DiD estimate: ${did_estimate}k")                  # DiD estimate: $3k
DiD fits most “some units changed, others didn’t” situations in marketing: store display pilots, shelf resets, regional promotion rollouts, pricing changes in selected markets, an app feature launched on one platform first.

The Parallel Trends Assumption
DiD rests on parallel trends (also called common trends): without the treatment, both groups would have followed the same trend. Trend, not level. The groups can start at different sales levels, as the pilot stores do. What matters is that the comparison group’s change after the rollout is a fair stand-in for what the pilot stores would have done on their own.
You can never fully verify that, because you don’t observe the pilot stores without the display. But you can check the period before the rollout.






Figure 3: Difference-in-Differences: pre-trends and divergence.



Plot both groups over time and look at the part before the display. If the two lines move together, DiD is credible. A clean pre-trend is a credibility check, not a proof, but it’s the check everyone will ask for.


When DiD doesn’t work
DiD fails when the sales team picked on momentum. If they chose stores that were already growing faster, the two groups don’t share a trend, and the DiD estimate takes credit for growth that was coming anyway. You’ll see it in the pre-period plot: the lines were already diverging before the display. When that happens, don’t force DiD. Match the groups more carefully, weight the comparison stores, or move to Synthetic Control.


Estimating DiD with a Regression
The two-by-two table is the idea. It isn’t what you’d report, for two reasons. It gives no standard error, so you can’t say whether +$3k is distinguishable from zero. And real data isn’t two periods; it’s 24 months of sales for 100 stores. The regression version handles both. One row per store per month, a fixed effect for each store, a fixed effect for each month, and one interaction term for treated stores in the post period. The store effects absorb every fixed difference between stores. The month effects absorb every trend and shock that hit all stores that month. The interaction term is the DiD estimate.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# df: one row per store-month (store_id, period, treated, post, category_sales)
model = smf.ols(
    "category_sales ~ C(store_id) + C(period) + treated:post",
    data=df,
).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["store_id"]})

coef, se = model.params["treated:post"], model.bse["treated:post"]
print(f"DiD estimate: {coef:.2f} (SE {se:.2f})")   # DiD estimate: 3.02 (SE 0.04)
Clustering the standard error by store handles the repeated measurements for each store. The same regression checks pre-trends: replace treated:post with one treated × month term per month and confirm the pre-rollout terms are close to zero. The companion notebook walks through the full panel and that check.

title: 3.3 Quasi Experiments
text:
Synthetic Control
Core idea: when no single control unit matches, build one by mixing several.
DiD worked because 50 control stores gave you a convincing trend to borrow. Now take the fourth row of Table 1: only the New York store got the display. Which of the other 99 stores is the right comparison? They differ in size, category mix, and local competition, and no single store is a convincing stand-in for New York.
Synthetic Control doesn’t pick one. It treats the other 99 stores as a donor pool and builds a “synthetic New York” as a weighted mix of them, choosing the weights so that the blend tracks New York’s sales as closely as possible before the display went in. In the companion notebook the blend comes out as 36% of the Boston store, 28% of Philadelphia, 22% of Chicago, and a few percent spread over four other stores. Once the display is in, the gap between actual New York and its synthetic twin is the estimated effect.






Figure 4: Synthetic Control: actual vs. synthetic counterfactual.



It’s the natural design whenever one unit gets the treatment and many similar units don’t: one store remodeled, one metro with an out-of-home campaign, one SKU with a price change and its sibling SKUs as donors. These geo-level designs come back in Section 6.3 as a robustness check for geo experiments and in Section 6.4 as the calibration anchor for media mix models.

When Synthetic Control doesn’t work
The credibility check is the pre-period fit. If no blend of the 99 stores can reproduce New York’s history before the display, don’t trust the gap after it. The donors also have to be untouched: a display in New York doesn’t move sales in Chicago, but a New York TV campaign might reach New Jersey, and a donor that caught the treatment drags the synthetic twin toward the treated path. And it can’t do one customer. A single customer’s weekly spend is mostly zeros and noise, and no blend of other customers will track it. Customer-level questions need many customers, which is DiD or RDD territory.

title: 3.3 Quasi Experiments
section: When There Is No Control Group
text:
When There Is No Control Group
DiD borrowed a trend from control stores. Synthetic Control blended control stores when no single one would do. RDD compared stores just below a line to stores just above it. All three borrow the comparison from units the action didn’t reach, and none of them can help when it reached everyone:

The new display went into all 100 stores on the same day.
The campaign ran in every region, not in a few.
The coupon went to every customer.

There’s no untreated store, region, or customer to compare against. So the comparison has to be forecast: from what the series was doing before the action, and from what other series the action couldn’t touch did after it. That’s the last rung of the ladder, CausalImpact, and it’s the next chapter.

title: 3.3 Quasi Experiments
text:
Key Takeaways

Start from how the treatment was assigned, not from the estimator. Random assignment gives you an A/B test. Anything else gives you a quasi-experiment, and the assignment picks which one.
RDD estimates a local effect for units near the cutoff, and only when there are many of them and none can move themselves across the line. Don’t read the jump at the threshold as an effect for everyone.
DiD exists because both naive comparisons fail. Before-versus-after books the market trend; treated-versus-control books the pre-existing gap. The difference of the differences cancels both, but only if the parallel trends assumption holds. Check the pre-period, and treat a clean pre-trend as a credibility check, not proof.
Synthetic Control stands or falls on the pre-period fit. If the weighted donor blend can’t reproduce the treated unit’s history, don’t trust the gap that follows.
DiD, Synthetic Control, and CausalImpact are a ladder: borrow the control’s trend, blend the controls, forecast the control. Each rung leans harder on a model. When the action reached every store, region, or customer, you’re on the last rung, which is the next chapter.

title: 3.4 Causal Impact with Time Series
text:
Building the Counterfactual
Every design in the previous chapter had a control group. Some stores got the display and some didn’t. One market got the campaign and the others didn’t. This chapter is for when there’s no control group at all.
A national TV campaign ran for eight weeks. Sales went up. But every market was exposed, so there’s no untreated market to compare against. What would sales have been without the campaign?
This chapter has one job: build that missing no-campaign path, and decide whether it’s credible enough to measure the campaign against. The building takes fifteen lines of code. Deciding whether to trust it is the rest of the chapter.
Core idea: forecast the sales you would have seen without the campaign. The effect is observed sales minus that forecast.
With no control group, the comparison has to come from time. Fit a time series model to sales before the campaign, so the campaign can’t leak into it. Project the model forward through the campaign window. That projection is the counterfactual, and the gap between it and what actually happened is the estimated effect.
The forecast can still use control series, and it’s worth being clear that these aren’t a control group. A control group is untreated units of the same kind: stores that didn’t get the display. A control series is a predictor: any series the campaign couldn’t have touched, such as a category demand index or a sibling product line with no media. It isn’t compared to the brand. It tells the forecast what the market was doing while the campaign ran.
The best-known implementation is CausalImpact, which Google released as an R package and Brodersen and colleagues described in a 2015 paper. In the causal inference literature the same design is called an interrupted time series. Python ports exist (tfp-causalimpact, and InterruptedTimeSeries in CausalPy). This chapter builds the same logic directly with statsmodels, so every assumption stays visible.
It’s the last rung of the ladder from the previous chapter, and the table shows what changed on the way up:
The worked example is a national CPG brand: four years of weekly revenue, an eight-week TV and PR campaign, and twenty weeks of observation after it. Two control series: a subcategory demand index and a sibling product line that got no media. The data is synthetic, so the true no-campaign path is known. Before any code, the brief:
That last line is a decision, and it’s made now, before anyone has seen a number. It’s why the forecast below runs 28 weeks, and why the reporting-window section later in the chapter is a check rather than a choice.
Here is the code that builds the counterfactual:
Three choices in that code matter. The model is fit on the pre-period only, so the campaign can’t contaminate its own baseline. Sales are modelled in logs, because a campaign lift and seasonality are both multiplicative, and the simulated paths are converted back to dollars before anything is summed. And the controls enter as regressors, so the forecast knows what the market did during the campaign. Whether the model also needs a trend term, or the controls at all, isn’t a matter of taste. The next section settles it by measurement.

Validating the Counterfactual Before Measuring
This step isn’t optional. The effect you’ll report is observed minus forecast, so every dollar of forecast error becomes a dollar of fake effect. Before using the forecast to measure the campaign, you have to show it can predict a period where nothing happened. Three checks do that, and all three run on the pre-period alone.

Backtesting the forecast
Can the model predict the untreated world? Pretend the campaign started at some earlier date inside the pre-period. Fit on the data before that date, forecast the next twenty-eight weeks, and compare to what actually happened. Repeat from several dates. Twenty-eight weeks because that’s the estimand in the brief, and a model that looks fine over eight weeks can fall apart over twenty-eight.

The controls cut the error in half, so on this data they earn their place. And the trend term matters at this horizon: the brand grows faster than its subcategory, and a model without a slope would charge that gap to the campaign.


Placebo interventions
Does the design invent effects when nothing happened? Pick a date in the pre-period, say week 120, when there was no campaign. Pretend one started that week and run the full analysis. The right answer is zero, so whatever comes back is what this design produces from noise. That’s a placebo intervention, and the nine backtest windows above double as nine placebos. The largest placebo effect here was $636k, and one of the nine returned an interval that excluded zero. Keep both numbers. The campaign estimate has to clear them.

Checking that the controls help
Do the controls actually improve the forecast? The backtest already said yes on this data, and it’s worth seeing what that buys. In a calm world the controls narrow the interval by a factor of twelve. When a category-wide dip hits three weeks of the campaign, the estimate with controls lands within 1.3% of the truth, because the counterfactual dips with the market. Without controls the same dip is charged to the campaign, and the estimate lands 21% below the truth. That’s what a good control series does: it absorbs shocks that hit everyone, so the model doesn’t mistake them for the campaign.
It only works if the campaign didn’t touch the control. That’s the assumption that can’t be tested from the data, and it gets its own section, When Not to Trust the Estimate.

How much to trust the interval

title: 3.4 Causal Impact with Time Series
section: When Not to Trust the Estimate
text:
When Not to Trust the Estimate
Three things break this analysis. Two of them leave no trace in the data.






Figure 4: What controls buy, and what breaks them




The campaign touched a control
The more predictive a control is, the more likely the campaign reached it. The subcategory index carries most of the model’s explanatory power, which is exactly why a national campaign for a large brand in that subcategory is a threat to it. Leak 35% of the brand’s lift into the index and the estimate keeps only 65% of the true effect, with an interval that no longer excludes zero. A campaign that worked now reads as inconclusive. And every diagnostic passes: the pre-period fit is clean, the interval is tight, the backtest looks the same. The violated assumption lives outside the data. The only way to check it is to ask the people who ran the campaign what it could have touched.


The pre-period relationship broke
A relationship that held for four years can still stop. Suppose a competitor enters and grows the subcategory by 5% in the post-period, and this brand doesn’t share in it. The controls now say the market got better, the counterfactual rises, and the estimate comes back at negative $460k against a true effect of positive $1,124k. It’s the only scenario in the chapter where the truth falls outside the interval, and it isn’t testable from pre-period data by construction. This is the same discipline DiD demands: the output is only as good as the claim that the controls kept behaving the way they did before.


The forecast was never good enough
The third failure does leave a trace, if you look. Run the same machinery on real Dunnhumby store data: take one store’s weekly sales, multiply the final twelve weeks by 1.15, and try to recover the planted lift with four other stores as controls.
The lift comes back. The planted 1,775 units are recovered as 1,833, with an interval that excludes zero. It would be easy to write that up as a successful controlled analysis.






Figure 5: Real controls that carry no information



It isn’t one. The cross-store correlation that justified the controls was 0.45, but the Dunnhumby panel starts small and grows, so every store rises together for reasons that have nothing to do with demand. Trim that onboarding ramp and the correlation falls to 0.01. The backtest settles it: adding the four control stores moves forecast error from 13.7% to 13.8%, which is to say not at all. The narrower interval is the trap. Extra regressors soak up in-sample variation and tighten the band even when the forecast didn’t improve. A narrower interval isn’t evidence that the controls helped. A better backtest is. What produced the number was a projection of one store’s own recent level, and a 13.7% forecast error is too weak to carry a causal claim. Saying so is the finding.

title: 3.4 Causal Impact with Time Series

A Practical Workflow
The chapter compresses to eight steps. Run them in order.

Write the brief. Business question, outcome, treatment, and the estimand with its reporting window. Fix it before you see a number.
Choose the control series. They have to be series the campaign couldn’t touch. Ask the people who ran it.
Fit on the pre-period only.
Backtest the counterfactual at the horizon you’ll report. Pick the specification from the backtest, not from taste.
Run placebo interventions. Know what the design returns from noise before you read the real number.
Estimate the post-period effect over the window you fixed in step 1.
Stress-test the controls. Could the campaign have reached them? Could the pre-period relationship have broken?
If the counterfactual is weak, don’t report a causal number. A 13.7% backtest error is a forecast, not a measurement.

CausalImpact doesn’t turn observational data into an experiment. It gives you a structured way to ask whether a time series can support a credible counterfactual. When it can’t, the answer isn’t a better model. It’s a better experiment next time (Chapter 6.3).

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
text:
Treatment Effects: ATE, CATE, ITE
The methods in previous chapters estimate one number for a whole group: the Average Treatment Effect (ATE), or the average impact of a treatment across everyone it reached. But in marketing, averages can be misleading. For example, a coupon might increase purchases by 5% on average, but that number hides the real story. Some customers might respond with a 20% lift, while others see no effect or even a drop. If you could identify which customers actually respond, you could spend your budget much more effectively.
Meta-learners try to estimate treatment effects for each individual customer. But what does that actually look like in practice?
To define the treatment effect, we turn to the Potential Outcomes Framework. The treatment effect is the difference in outcomes caused by a treatment: formally, \(\tau = Y(1) - Y(0)\), where \(Y(1)\) is the outcome under treatment and \(Y(0)\) is the outcome under control. For example, if the potential purchase rate with a coupon is 20% and the rate without it is 10%, the treatment effect is 10%.
Now, there are three levels of granularity:
Why does this matter? Because not all customers behave the same way. A price-sensitive customer might jump at a discount, while a brand-loyal customer would have bought at full price anyway. If you know who is who, you can target discounts where they actually drive extra sales, instead of giving away margin to customers who would have purchased regardless.

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
text:
Figure 1: The treatment effect as a difference in potential outcomes.





ATE (Average Treatment Effect): the effect averaged across all customers. “Did the coupon increase sales?”
CATE (Conditional Average Treatment Effect): the average effect for customers with specific characteristics. “Did the coupon work better for urban customers under 30?”
ITE (Individual Treatment Effect): the effect for a specific individual. Unobservable in practice, but CATE provides our best estimate.
crumbs: 10  3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
text:
Why We Need Meta Learners
Consider this question: did a coupon increase sales? To answer it, we look at data from various customers, including their attributes (age, gender, location), the treatment (coupon or no coupon), and the outcome (purchase or not).
The column \(Y(1)\) represents the outcome when the coupon is used, while \(Y(0)\) represents the outcome without the coupon. If we had both columns for the same individual, calculating the treatment effect would be as simple as subtracting one from the other. But the challenge is that we can only observe one outcome for each individual.






Figure 2: The missing counterfactual: only one outcome is observed per customer.



To solve this, we use meta-learners. These are machine learning frameworks that predict what would have happened if a customer had received the other treatment. By filling in these missing counterfactuals, we can estimate the treatment effect for each person.
crumbs: 10  3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
section: S-Learner: Start with a Single Model
text:
S-Learner: Start with a Single Model
The “S” in S-learner stands for “Single,” because it relies on a single machine learning model. We train it on all the data, with the treatment indicator included as just another feature. To estimate the effect for a customer with characteristics \(x\), we ask that one model for two predictions:
\[\hat{Y}(1 \mid X=x) = \text{predicted outcome if treated}\]
\[\hat{Y}(0 \mid X=x) = \text{predicted outcome if not treated}\]
The estimated treatment effect is the difference between them:
\[\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{Y}(1 \mid X=x) - \hat{Y}(0 \mid X=x)\]
In code, the S-learner gets these two predictions from the same model: once with the treatment set to 1, and once with it set to 0.






Figure 3: S-learner: one model predicts both potential outcomes.



Pseudo-code:
# Train a single model with treatment as a feature
X = df[['age', 'gender', 'location', 'treatment']]
y = df['sales']

model = xgb.XGBRegressor()
model.fit(X, y)

df['sales_treated'] = model.predict(X.assign(treatment=1))
df['sales_control'] = model.predict(X.assign(treatment=0))

df['treatment_effect'] = df['sales_treated'] - df['sales_control']
ATE = df['treatment_effect'].mean()
S-learner is the simplest way to start, and often a reasonable baseline. But it has a key weakness: if the treatment effect is small compared to other features, the model can end up ignoring the treatment variable, especially if you use regularization. This means your CATE estimates can be biased toward zero.
crumbs: 10  3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
text:
T-Learner: Two Separate Models
The “T” in T-learner stands for “Two.” Instead of one model, we train two separate models: one on the treated group and one on the control group. We get \(\hat{Y}(1 \mid X=x)\) from the treated model and \(\hat{Y}(0 \mid X=x)\) from the control model, then take the difference:
\[\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{Y}(1 \mid X=x) - \hat{Y}(0 \mid X=x)\]






Figure 4: T-learner: separate models fill each potential-outcome column.



Pseudo-code:
df_treated = df[df['treatment'] == 1]
df_control = df[df['treatment'] == 0]

# Train separate models, one per arm
model_treated = xgb.XGBRegressor()
model_treated.fit(df_treated[['age', 'gender', 'location']], df_treated['sales'])

model_control = xgb.XGBRegressor()
model_control.fit(df_control[['age', 'gender', 'location']], df_control['sales'])

df['sales_treated'] = model_treated.predict(df[['age', 'gender', 'location']])
df['sales_control'] = model_control.predict(df[['age', 'gender', 'location']])

df['treatment_effect'] = df['sales_treated'] - df['sales_control']
ATE = df['treatment_effect'].mean()
T-learner is more flexible because each model can learn different patterns for treated and control groups. But there is a tradeoff: it can have high variance, especially if your treatment and control groups are imbalanced. When you subtract the predictions, errors from both models can add up.
So, S-learner is simple but tends to underestimate effects. T-learner avoids that particular failure, at the cost of noisier estimates. What can we do next?

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
text:
Advanced Meta-Learners
Beyond S and T, several more sophisticated methods address their limitations:

X-Learner: An extension of T-learner designed for imbalanced treatment groups. It imputes the missing counterfactuals and combines them using propensity-score weighting. Works well when one group is much larger than the other.
DR-Learner (Doubly Robust): Combines outcome modeling and propensity score estimation. Consistent if either model is correctly specified, hence “doubly robust.”
DML (Double Machine Learning): Uses cross-fitting to avoid overfitting bias, with strong theoretical guarantees. More computationally expensive, roughly an order of magnitude slower than the S-learner in the companion notebook, but provides proper confidence intervals.







Figure 5: Meta-learner methods, from simple to complex.



Theory tells us what each method is supposed to optimize. But the real test is seeing how they perform on the same dataset, where you can see the practical differences.

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
text:
Example: Estimating Heterogeneous Email Effects
To see how these methods behave, we need a dataset where we can check their work. That is harder than it sounds. In real data we never observe a customer’s true treatment effect, so we cannot tell whether a meta-learner recovered the right pattern or just produced plausible noise.
We solve this with a semi-synthetic example built on Kevin Hillstrom’s MineThatData email experiment, a classic marketing dataset of 64,000 customers randomized to a men’s-merchandise email, a women’s email, or no email. We keep the real customer features (recency, purchase history, channel, and the rest) and the real randomized assignment for the binary contrast of men’s email versus no email. Only the outcomes are simulated: we define a baseline purchase probability and a treatment effect \(\tau(x)\) that is larger for men’s-merchandise buyers, recently active customers, and multichannel shoppers. Because we wrote \(\tau(x)\) ourselves, we know each customer’s true CATE and can grade every learner against it.
This is a teaching device. The goal is not to estimate the average effect better than the experiment already does, but to check whether a meta-learner recovers the heterogeneity we planted.

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
section: What to Check Before Trusting CATE
text:
What to Check Before Trusting CATE
This example was forgiving by design: randomized treatment, perfect overlap, and a known answer. Real projects rarely are. Before you act on CATE estimates:

A meta-learner does not create a causal comparison. It models how the effect varies inside one you already have, so on observational data the CATE inherits every confounding problem the underlying comparison carries.
The individual treatment effect is never observed in real data. We could grade the learners here only because we simulated the truth.
CATE is a model estimate, not a measurement. Read it at the group or segment level, not as a literal number for one customer.
Sanity-check the average. If the mean estimated CATE is far from a simple difference in means on an experiment, something is wrong.
Check stability across learners. If S, T, X, and the causal forest disagree on the ranking, trust none of them yet.
Watch overlap. Where treated and control customers do not coexist, CATE is an extrapolation rather than an estimate.

title: 3.5 Meta Learners for Treatment Effects
text:
Key Takeaways

ATE answers “did it work on average”; CATE asks “for whom did it work.” Targeting needs the second, and meta-learners estimate it by using machine learning to fill in each customer’s missing counterfactual.
S-learner is the simplest baseline but can bias effects toward zero when the treatment signal is weak; T-learner avoids that shared-model failure at the cost of higher variance. X-, DR-, and DML-learners trade extra machinery for robustness to treatment imbalance and to errors in the fitted models, but none of them repairs confounding you did not measure.
Which learner ranks customers best is data-dependent. Grade recovery on your own data, with a semi-synthetic benchmark if needed, rather than trusting any method by reputation.
CATE is a group-level model estimate, not a per-customer measurement. Run the checks above, from the mean against the experimental difference to learner stability and overlap, before spending budget on it.
